=== DISCLOSURE ===
# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

Handheld vacuum lifter with grip-loss alarm

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter includes a rigid body with a handle and a suction cup that carries a flexible sealing lip. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port to create a vacuum. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum and drives a warning indicator when vacuum is lost. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump. The warning indicator is configured to activate before a load can be dropped.

1. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter comprising:
    a rigid body comprising a handle;
    a suction cup carried by the rigid body, the suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip;
    an electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body, the electric vacuum pump configured to draw air through a port to create a vacuum;
    a pressure sensor configured to monitor the vacuum;
    a warning indicator driven by the pressure sensor, the warning indicator configured to activate when the vacuum is lost; and
    a rechargeable battery configured to power the electric vacuum pump.

2. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter of claim 1, wherein the warning indicator is configured to activate before a load can be dropped.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter for glass and stone panels is disclosed. The lifter includes a suction cup 10 that carries a flexible sealing lip 12 on a rigid body 14. The rigid body 14 also includes a handle 16. An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a vacuum. A pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum. The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before a load can be dropped. A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20.
=== BRIEF ===
# Drafting brief

- Working title: Cordless Handheld Vacuum Lifter With Grip-Loss Warning Indicator
- Applicant: (not supplied)
- Named inventors: Nimo Rotem
- Starting point: a description of the invention in the inventor's own words
- Prior-art search: adhoc-6a686e4569e2

## Inventor and filing notes

Filing and drafting instructions:
No domestic or foreign priority claim was supplied. Use 'Not applicable.' in the cross-reference section.
No government support was supplied. Use 'Not applicable.' in the government support section.
Use a broad, disclosure-supported independent claim with a graduated fallback ladder.
Use every statutory claim class the disclosure genuinely supports.
Avoid means-plus-function language unless the user later requests it.
=== CONVERSATION ===
# Conversation so far

### USER

Here is my invention.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter includes a rigid body with a handle and a suction cup that carries a flexible sealing lip. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port to create a vacuum. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum and drives a warning indicator when vacuum is lost. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump. The warning indicator is configured to activate before a load can be dropped.

    a rigid body comprising a handle;
    a suction cup carried by the rigid body, the suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip;
    an electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body, the electric vacuum pump configured to draw air through a port to create a vacuum;
    a pressure sensor configured to monitor the vacuum;
    a warning indicator driven by the pressure sensor, the warning indicator configured to activate when the vacuum is lost; and
    a rechargeable battery configured to power the electric vacuum pump.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter for glass and stone panels is disclosed. The lifter includes a suction cup 10 that carries a flexible sealing lip 12 on a rigid body 14. The rigid body 14 also includes a handle 16. An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a vacuum. A pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum. The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before a load can be dropped. A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20.

### YOU (the drafting agent)

The first working draft is written: all nine sections in draft/, a 33-entry reference-numeral table, and five figure files in figures/.

The drafting problem worth knowing about is this. The claim 1 in your disclosure is, element for element, what US-10625955-B2 already claims — a main body with a handle, sealing units bounding a sealed space, a vacuum pump, a pressure sensing unit, a rechargeable battery charged from external equipment, and a warning unit — and CN-110630621-B is its near-twin. So I could not use that claim as written.

What I used instead is the one thing you say that none of the five references does: the indicator activates *before a load can be dropped*. In claim 1 that is now a recited relationship rather than an aspiration — the warning vacuum level is greater than the release vacuum level at which the cup lets go, so a decaying grip crosses the warning level first and the indicator fires while the cup is still holding. 1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.
12	
13	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.
14	
15	A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colors which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. The sufficiency indicated in that device is determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source rather than from a measurement of the vacuum holding the object.
16	
17	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.
18	
19	A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. 20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	Third, the remedies that the known equipment applies to a failing grip are remedies a cordless handheld lifter does not have. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.
26	
27	There remains a need for a cordless handheld vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

13	Abstract: A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers during the manufacture of integrated circuits. The wand device comprises a housing having a hollow interior and a tip for grasping objects. The tip is attached to the housing through a hollow tube, and has a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal when placed against the surface of an object to be grasped. The tip also has a recessed interior region having an air inlet therein. The wand device includes a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing. The vacuum pump produces a suction force at the air inlet on the tip. When the tip is placed against the surface of an object, the object is securely grasped due to the suction force exerted thereon by the wand tip. A switch located on the wand may be used to turn the vacuum pump on or off in order to grasp or release the object. Light-emitting diodes of different colors indicate to an operator whether or not the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object.

Abstract: An electric sucker comprises a body, a vacuum pump, a pressure sensing unit and a start key. When the user presses the activation key, the vacuum pump will act to pump out the air between the electric sucker and the component attached to the electric sucker, so that the electric sucker is adsorbed on the component. The pressure sensing unit can detect the pressure between the electric sucker and the component in real time. When the pressure sensing unit detects that the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component is lower than a second preset pressure, the vacuum pump automatically acts to pump out the air between the electric suction cup and the component again. After the user sets up the electric chuck on the component that wants to adsorb, can make the electric chuck adsorb automatically on simply through pressing the start key on the component. Then, the electric suction cup can automatically detect the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component in real time, and automatically perform air suction again when the pressure is lower than a second preset pressure, so that the safety of related personnel using the electric suction cup can be ensured.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 activates while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

That timing answers a technical problem that arises when a suction grip decays in the hand. The decay is progressive and, to the person holding the load, silent: nothing in the feel of the tool changes until the suction cup 10 lets go. A device that treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be answered by running its pump again fixes the value at which it acts by reference to the vacuum it is trying to maintain, and that value says nothing about how much grip is left; when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, the pump runs while the grip continues to decay and the person carrying the load is told nothing. A signal derived instead from the state of the power source, from how fast the vacuum is changing, or from a number that the user must read off a display while carrying a load reports something other than whether the load is about to be released. The activation of the warning indicator 32 is tied to the retention of the load: it occurs while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

The distinction does real work on a tool that is carried in the hand. Vacuum handling equipment that hangs from a frame can answer a failing grip with a further vacuum source or by refusing to move. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has no such remedy available to it. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person whose hand is on the handle 16, and that person can act only if the notice arrives while the suction cup 10 retains the load, with grip remaining to bring the load down.

The pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained on the suction cup 10 and carried by the handle 16, and the warning indicator 32 activates while the load is carried by the handle 16.

The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32 without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries. The electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1.

FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, the port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost, and is configured to activate before the load can be dropped.

The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried.

The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a lifting step 205, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the panel 50. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum. At the lifting step 205, the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon loss of the grip vacuum, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. The activating step 208 occurs before the panel 50 can be dropped.

9	The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 activates while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

11	That timing answers a technical problem that arises when a suction grip decays in the hand. The decay is progressive and, to the person holding the load, silent: nothing in the feel of the tool changes until the suction cup 10 lets go. A device that treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be answered by running its pump again fixes the value at which it acts by reference to the vacuum it is trying to maintain, and that value says nothing about how much grip is left; when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, the pump runs while the grip continues to decay and the person carrying the load is told nothing. A signal derived instead from the state of the power source, from how fast the vacuum is changing, or from a number that the user must read off a display while carrying a load reports something other than whether the load is about to be released. The activation of the warning indicator 32 is tied to the retention of the load: it occurs while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person whose hand is on the handle 16, and that person can act only if the notice arrives while the suction cup 10 retains the load, with grip remaining to bring the load down.

The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries. The electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1.

FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, the port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 activates while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

That timing answers a technical problem that arises when a suction grip decays in the hand. The decay is progressive and, to the person holding the load, silent: nothing in the feel of the tool changes until the suction cup 10 lets go. A device that treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be answered by running its pump again fixes the value at which it acts by reference to the vacuum it is trying to maintain, and that value says nothing about how much grip is left; when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, the pump runs while the grip continues to decay and the person carrying the load is told nothing. A signal derived instead from the state of the power source, from how fast the vacuum is changing, or from a number that the user must read off a display while carrying a load reports something other than whether the load is about to be released. The activation of the warning indicator 32 is tied to the retention of the load: it occurs while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

The distinction does real work on a tool that is carried in the hand. Vacuum handling equipment that hangs from a frame can answer a failing grip with a further vacuum source or by refusing to move. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has no such remedy available to it. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person whose hand is on the handle 16, and that person can act only if the notice arrives while the suction cup 10 retains the load, with grip remaining to bring the load down.

The pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained on the suction cup 10 and carried by the handle 16, and the warning indicator 32 activates while the load is carried by the handle 16.

The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32 without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried.

The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a lifting step 205, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the panel 50. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum. At the lifting step 205, the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon loss of the grip vacuum, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. The activating step 208 occurs while the suction cup 10 retains the panel 50, before the panel 50 can be dropped, and while the panel 50 is carried by the handle 16.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

That device monitors and maintains negative pressure in real time and shows the negative pressure value and the battery power on the display screen as numbers for the user to read.

-Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

+Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1]. That equipment is frame-mounted rather than hand-carried, its controller cycles the vacuum pump on the pressure data to maintain a partial vacuum at a setpoint vacuum pressure, and the indicators are described as indicating a functional condition of a module rather than as being timed with respect to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the workpiece.

Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the person carrying the panel is given no signal that is tied to the vacuum still needed to hold it. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a determination made from the state of the power source, on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

input.summary: Both independent claims now recite the warning-timing relationship the search found nowhere in the art: the warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum is lost AND while the suction cup retains the load, before the load can be dropped. The detailed description carries that feature in the same words and adds two paragraphs stating the technical problem it solves (a grip that decays silently in the hand, a pump-restart value fixed by reference to the vacuum the pump is trying to maintain, and the fact that the only actuator available to a hand-carried lifter is the person on the handle). Both reviewer findings were genuine and are fixed: the causal "such that / so that" link between the battery-to-pump connection and cordless monitoring and warning is replaced with coordinate statements in the claim, description, summary and abstract, and the description, summary and abstract now use the claim's own vocabulary ("creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator") instead of "grips, monitors, and warns". One sentence was added to the Background so the peripheral WO-2022236379-A1 teaching is stated with the reason it does not bear on the claimed combination. No numerals, figures, or figure briefs needed to change.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries a single added relationship rather than a pile of limitations: the warning indicator is configured to activate when the grip vacuum is lost AND while the suction cup retains the load, before the load can be dropped. This is the inventor's own claim-2 subject matter promoted into claim 1, so nothing was invented to get it.

That feature is what clears claim 1 of US-10625955-B2 and CN-110630621-B, the two references whose apparatus recitations otherwise track the inventor's claim 1 element for element. In both, the pressure comparison is a high/low pair that stops and restarts the pump, the low predetermined pressure being a restart value fixed by reference to the vacuum being maintained; the on-tool warning unit of US-10625955-B2 is operated on low battery power, and pressure-related warning information is transmitted to an external electronic device. Neither times an activation of an indicator by reference to the load still being retained.

The same feature clears US-10518985-B2 (warning when a rate of vacuum level change exceeds a threshold rate), US-5310232-A (malfunction alarm when a preset limit pressure is exceeded on a plate assembly whose answer to a failing grip is a battery-fed emergency vacuum source), WO-2017156581-A1 (an attach indicator activated when vacuum is greater than a preselected safe level, with a below-minimum vacuum answered by running the pump), US-5184858-A (sound generator switched on when a manually generated vacuum reaches a predetermined value), US-5374090-A (sufficiency determined from voltage drop across resistors across the power source, not from a vacuum measurement), CN-2806399-Y (buzzer according to different usage states, with continued pumping as the safety measure), US-2024424646-A1 (negative-pressure and battery numbers on a display for the user to read), and WO-2022236379-A1 (frame-mounted modules cycled to a setpoint vacuum pressure, indicators showing a module's functional condition).

Method claim 5 recites the same relationship in method terms: activating the warning indicator upon loss of the grip vacuum and while the suction cup retains the panel, before the panel can be dropped, after monitoring while the panel is retained on the suction cup. It is infringed by the user of the tool rather than its maker, so the two classes reach different parties.

I did NOT put the search's other unmatched element, the single-hand design with everything on the rigid body and no external hose or cord, into claim 1. US-5374090-A is expressly a cordless device with the power source and the vacuum pump positioned within the housing, so cordlessness alone would not carry claim 1, and the disclosure never says where the pressure sensor and the warning indicator sit, so a claim that all components are carried by the rigid body would not be supported. Untethered whole-tool operation is kept where it is defensible, as apparatus claim 2 and method claim 7.

I also did not reinstate any threshold architecture: no working vacuum level, no release vacuum level, no ordering of levels, no numeric values. The inventor says only that the indicator warns before a load can be dropped. Claim 1 states that as a timing relationship in the inventor's own words plus the retention it entails, which is the strongest form the disclosure actually supports. The contrast with a value fixed by reference to the vacuum the pump is trying to maintain is placed in the description as the technical problem, where a later argument can be built from it, without being claimed as a structure.

The ladder now descends: claim 1 (timing tied to retention), claim 2 (whole tool creates, monitors and warns with no cord to an external supply, the reason the person on the handle is the only available actuator), claim 3 (monitoring and warning continue while the load is carried by the handle, which is the interval that matters and is separately arguable over attach-time indicators), claim 4 (glass or stone panel against the sealing lip). Method claims 6 to 8 mirror the panel, cordless and while-carried fallbacks.

Both reviewer findings were correct and were fixed rather than argued with. The battery-to-pump connection and cordless operation are now coordinate statements, not cause and effect, and the three acts are named identically in claims, description, summary and abstract.

That is the one relationship none of the ten references discloses: the powered suction devices fix the value at which they act by reference to the vacuum the pump is maintaining and then restart the pump, the frame-scale equipment alarms on a preset limit, a rate of change, or a module condition and answers with a further vacuum source, and the remaining indicators report power-source sufficiency, usage state, an attach-time go signal, or numbers on a display. data.summary: Both independent claims now recite the warning-timing relationship the search found nowhere in the art: the warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum is lost AND while the suction cup retains the load, before the load can be dropped. The detailed description carries that feature in the same words and adds two paragraphs stating the technical problem it solves (a grip that decays silently in the hand, a pump-restart value fixed by reference to the vacuum the pump is trying to maintain, and the fact that the only actuator available to a hand-carried lifter is the person on the handle). Both reviewer findings were genuine and are fixed: the causal "such that / so that" link between the battery-to-pump connection and cordless monitoring and warning is replaced with coordinate statements in the claim, description, summary and abstract, and the description, summary and abstract now use the claim's own vocabulary ("creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator") instead of "grips, monitors, and warns". One sentence was added to the Background so the peripheral WO-2022236379-A1 teaching is stated with the reason it does not bear on the claimed combination. No numerals, figures, or figure briefs needed to change.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries a single added relationship rather than a pile of limitations: the warning indicator is configured to activate when the grip vacuum is lost AND while the suction cup retains the load, before the load can be dropped. This is the inventor's own claim-2 subject matter promoted into claim 1, so nothing was invented to get it.

That feature is what clears claim 1 of US-10625955-B2 and CN-110630621-B, the two references whose apparatus recitations otherwise track the inventor's claim 1 element for element. In both, the pressure comparison is a high/low pair that stops and restarts the pump, the low predetermined pressure being a restart value fixed by reference to the vacuum being maintained; the on-tool warning unit of US-10625955-B2 is operated on low battery power, and pressure-related warning information is transmitted to an external electronic device. Neither times an activation of an indicator by reference to the load still being retained.

The same feature clears US-10518985-B2 (warning when a rate of vacuum level change exceeds a threshold rate), US-5310232-A (malfunction alarm when a preset limit pressure is exceeded on a plate assembly whose answer to a failing grip is a battery-fed emergency vacuum source), WO-2017156581-A1 (an attach indicator activated when vacuum is greater than a preselected safe level, with a below-minimum vacuum answered by running the pump), US-5184858-A (sound generator switched on when a manually generated vacuum reaches a predetermined value), US-5374090-A (sufficiency determined from voltage drop across resistors across the power source, not from a vacuum measurement), CN-2806399-Y (buzzer according to different usage states, with continued pumping as the safety measure), US-2024424646-A1 (negative-pressure and battery numbers on a display for the user to read), and WO-2022236379-A1 (frame-mounted modules cycled to a setpoint vacuum pressure, indicators showing a module's functional condition).

Method claim 5 recites the same relationship in method terms: activating the warning indicator upon loss of the grip vacuum and while the suction cup retains the panel, before the panel can be dropped, after monitoring while the panel is retained on the suction cup. It is infringed by the user of the tool rather than its maker, so the two classes reach different parties.

I did NOT put the search's other unmatched element, the single-hand design with everything on the rigid body and no external hose or cord, into claim 1. US-5374090-A is expressly a cordless device with the power source and the vacuum pump positioned within the housing, so cordlessness alone would not carry claim 1, and the disclosure never says where the pressure sensor and the warning indicator sit, so a claim that all components are carried by the rigid body would not be supported. Untethered whole-tool operation is kept where it is defensible, as apparatus claim 2 and method claim 7.

I also did not reinstate any threshold architecture: no working vacuum level, no release vacuum level, no ordering of levels, no numeric values. The inventor says only that the indicator warns before a load can be dropped. Claim 1 states that as a timing relationship in the inventor's own words plus the retention it entails, which is the strongest form the disclosure actually supports. The contrast with a value fixed by reference to the vacuum the pump is trying to maintain is placed in the description as the technical problem, where a later argument can be built from it, without being claimed as a structure.

The ladder now descends: claim 1 (timing tied to retention), claim 2 (whole tool creates, monitors and warns with no cord to an external supply, the reason the person on the handle is the only available actuator), claim 3 (monitoring and warning continue while the load is carried by the handle, which is the interval that matters and is separately arguable over attach-time indicators), claim 4 (glass or stone panel against the sealing lip). Method claims 6 to 8 mirror the panel, cordless and while-carried fallbacks.

Both reviewer findings were correct and were fixed rather than argued with. The battery-to-pump connection and cordless operation are now coordinate statements, not cause and effect, and the three acts are named identically in claims, description, summary and abstract.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries. The electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1.

FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, the port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 activates while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

That timing answers a technical problem that arises when a suction grip decays in the hand. The decay is progressive and, to the person holding the load, silent: nothing in the feel of the tool changes until the suction cup 10 lets go. A device that treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be answered by running its pump again fixes the value at which it acts by reference to the vacuum it is trying to maintain, and that value says nothing about how much grip is left; when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, the pump runs while the grip continues to decay and the person carrying the load is told nothing. A signal derived instead from the state of the power source, from how fast the vacuum is changing, or from a number that the user must read off a display while carrying a load reports something other than whether the load is about to be released. The activation of the warning indicator 32 is tied to the retention of the load: it occurs while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

The distinction does real work on a tool that is carried in the hand. Vacuum handling equipment that hangs from a frame can answer a failing grip with a further vacuum source or by refusing to move. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has no such remedy available to it. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person whose hand is on the handle 16, and that person can act only if the notice arrives while the suction cup 10 retains the load, with grip remaining to bring the load down.

The pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained on the suction cup 10 and carried by the handle 16, and the warning indicator 32 activates while the load is carried by the handle 16.

The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32 without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried.

The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a lifting step 205, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the panel 50. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum. At the lifting step 205, the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon loss of the grip vacuum, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. The activating step 208 occurs while the suction cup 10 retains the panel 50, before the panel 50 can be dropped, and while the panel 50 is carried by the handle 16.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries. An electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1.

FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, a port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 activates while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

That timing answers a technical problem that arises when a suction grip decays in the hand. The decay is progressive and, to the person holding the load, silent: nothing in the feel of the tool changes until the suction cup 10 lets go. A device that treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be answered by running its pump again fixes the value at which it acts by reference to the vacuum it is trying to maintain, and that value says nothing about how much grip is left; when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, the pump runs while the grip continues to decay and the person carrying the load is told nothing. A signal derived instead from the state of the power source, from how fast the vacuum is changing, or from a number that the user must read off a display while carrying a load reports something other than whether the load is about to be released. The activation of the warning indicator 32 is tied to the retention of the load: it occurs while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

The distinction does real work on a tool that is carried in the hand. Vacuum handling equipment that is not carried in the hand can answer a failing grip with a further vacuum source, or by limiting or altering machine functions. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has no such remedy available to it. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person whose hand is on the handle 16, and that person can act only if the notice arrives while the suction cup 10 retains the load, with grip remaining to bring the load down.

The pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained on the suction cup 10 and carried by the handle 16, and the warning indicator 32 activates while the load is carried by the handle 16.
